nodes.label: Hybrid canes
nodes.full: On the mainland New Guinea cane meets wild S. spontaneum and hybrids arise — S. barberi in north India and S. sinense in south China — that suit cooler lands and push commercial cane from about 25°N to 35°N.

nodes.label: Atharvaveda
nodes.full: Sugarcane is absent from the Rigveda and first recorded about 1000 BC in the Atharvaveda, possibly recognising a cultigen already present in pre-Aryan Bengal.

nodes.label: Pātimokkha
nodes.full: The monks’ rule codified in the Buddha’s lifetime allows syrup (phāṇita) to the sick as one of the five medicines.

nodes.label: Ikṣvāku
nodes.full: The Buddha is later called ‘born of sugarcane’ because the Śākya clan traced its descent to Ikṣvāku; Buddhist literature mentions cane widely from about 500 BC.

nodes.label: Guḍa
nodes.full: About 300 BC the expanded Vinaya and the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra name guḍa, lump sugar, after syrup — the second rung of the Indian ladder.

nodes.label: Indus satrapy
nodes.full: Darius I makes the Indus valley a Persian satrapy and sends Scylax down the river to Egypt.
nodes.src: Achaemenid folio; Buttery (2022) p.8 for the sugar claim

nodes.label: Alexander at Indus
nodes.full: Alexander’s army reaches the Punjab and sends Nearchus down the Indus: the Greeks’ first direct contact with India.

nodes.label: Nearchus
nodes.full: Nearchus reports reeds that yield honey though there are no bees, preserved in Strabo.

edges: On the Brandes model S. officinarum had reached India and hybridised by the time the Atharvaveda names the cane about 1000 BC, though the verse may record an older Bengal cultigen.
Daniels sets the sequence directly: syrup (phāṇita) in the Pātimokkha about 500 BC, then amorphous lump sugar (guḍa) about 300 BC in the expanded Vinaya.
Both are early Buddhist uses of cane — the monks’ syrup and the founder’s ‘sugarcane’ lineage — in the literature Daniels dates from about 500 BC.
Alexander marches into Indus lands that Darius I had already made a Persian satrapy.
Nearchus’s report comes from the fleet that Alexander sent down the Indus; Bouras-Vallianatos says the Greeks first met cane juice on that campaign.
